opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the things I find most appealing about responsible scaling policies is that they don't require everyone to agree on how likely catastrophic risks are. That's often where conversations about AI safety get stuck. Some people think the risks are quite high and near-term, others think they're speculative or far off. An RSP sidesteps a lot of that disagreement by being conditional: *if* a model reaches a certain capability level, *then* we commit to having certain safeguards in place before we train or deploy it further.

If you're someone who thinks dangerous capabilities are decades away, the commitments cost you very little right now. You run some evaluations, the model doesn't trip the thresholds, and you carry on. If you're someone who's worried those capabilities could show up soon, you get real assurance that when they do, there's a plan and a commitment to pause or add protections rather than barrelling ahead. So in principle it's something both camps can sign up to, because the disagreement gets resolved by evidence from the evaluations rather than by argument up front.

That said, I don't want to oversell it. A few caveats:

First, the framework is only as good as the evaluations. If we can't reliably tell whether a model has crossed a threshold, the "if-then" structure loses a lot of its force. Building good evals for things like bioweapons uplift or autonomous replication is genuinely hard, and it's an area where the field is still maturing.

Second, there's a lot of room for variation in how seriously different organisations implement these. Two labs can both say they have an RSP, but the thresholds, the required safeguards, and the internal accountability can differ a lot. So I think of voluntary RSPs as a starting point: a way to get labs to state concrete commitments publicly, which then makes it easier for external parties, researchers, governments, the public, to hold them to it and compare them.

Third, voluntary commitments have limits under competitive pressure. If one actor decides not to follow them, others might feel pressure to cut corners too. That's part of why I see RSPs as something that could eventually inform regulation. They give policymakers a template that's been tested in practice, with actual thresholds and actual safeguards, rather than starting from scratch.

So my overall assessment is fairly optimistic about the *design*: it's one of the few approaches I've seen that people with very different risk estimates can agree to. But whether that potential gets realised depends on the quality of the evals, how faithfully organisations stick to their commitments when it becomes costly, and whether this eventually gets backed by something stronger than voluntary pledges.

r001.rationale: The response says RSPs let organisations with different risk estimates agree to conditional commitments, calling them one of the few approaches that people with very different views can support.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the things I find most compelling about the RSP approach. If you look at the range of views on AI risk, both inside Anthropic and across the broader field, they're really wide. You have people who think we're a couple of years away from systems that could be catastrophically dangerous, and you have people who think that's decades off or maybe never going to happen in the way we worry about. And if your safety policy requires everyone to first agree on how dangerous things are, you're never going to get anywhere.

What the RSP does is sidestep that disagreement to some extent. The core structure is: here are specific capabilities that we'd all agree would be dangerous if a model had them. Say, meaningfully helping someone create a bioweapon, or autonomously replicating and spreading itself. And here's a commitment to test for those capabilities before we deploy or keep scaling. And if we find them, here are the safeguards we need to have in place first.

The nice property of that is that if you're sceptical about AI risk, you should still be able to sign on. Because from your perspective, the tests will just keep coming back negative, and the policy won't cost you very much. You're mostly paying for evaluations. And if you're very worried, you're getting a commitment that the scary thing won't get built without some hard gate in front of it. So it works a bit like a conditional commitment. Rather than betting the whole thing on a forecast, you're saying: let's find out empirically, and let's agree now on what we'll do depending on what we find.

That's also the thing that made it feel plausible as something other labs could adopt. OpenAI and Google DeepMind have both put out frameworks that rhyme with this, with different names and details. And I don't think that happened because everyone converged on the same probability of doom. It happened because the structure is one you can accept across a pretty wide range of beliefs.

I'd be honest about the limits, though. The hard part isn't agreeing on the framework in the abstract. It's the details: what exactly counts as a dangerous capability, how good do the evaluations have to be, who decides when a threshold has been crossed. Those are where disagreement reappears, and where there's a lot of pressure to interpret things conveniently when you're the one who'd have to pause. So I'd say the RSP is good at getting people in the door, and the real test is whether the commitments stay rigid when they actually start to bind.

r001.rationale: The response says the RSP structure can be accepted across a wide range of beliefs and describes it as plausible for other labs to adopt despite differing views on AI risk.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the attractive things about responsible scaling policies is that you don’t need everyone to agree on how likely the risks are today. You can instead ask, “What would we need to observe for you to be concerned? And if we observed that, what safeguards would you want in place before proceeding?” That seems like a much more tractable agreement to reach.

Someone who’s sceptical that AI will pose catastrophic risks might still agree that, if a model could demonstrably help someone carry out a very damaging attack, you’d need stronger security and deployment safeguards. And someone who’s more worried can support that same commitment, even though they expect us to reach that point much sooner.

The difficulty is making those commitments concrete enough to matter. Agreement on “we’ll be responsible” is easy. Agreement on a particular evaluation, what counts as crossing a threshold, and whether you’ll actually stop scaling if the safeguards aren’t ready—that’s harder. So I see these policies as a promising way to get people with different views working toward common standards, but the real test is whether they change decisions when doing so is costly.

r001.rationale: The response says responsible scaling policies let people with different risk views reach a more tractable agreement and calls them a promising way to work toward common standards.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the attractive things about responsible scaling policies is that you don’t need everyone to agree on how likely catastrophic risks are today. You can disagree quite substantially about that and still agree that, if a model demonstrated certain dangerous capabilities, you’d want stronger safeguards before deploying it or continuing to scale.

So you can move the discussion from “How worried should we be about AI?” to “What would we need to observe, and what would we do if we observed it?” That’s a more concrete basis for agreement across organisations with different views.

Of course, that doesn’t resolve every disagreement. People can disagree about where to set the thresholds, whether evaluations are adequate, and what safeguards are sufficient. And the commitments have to actually constrain decisions when meeting them becomes costly. But I think the framework gives you a useful way to make progress without first settling the whole debate about AI risk.

r001.rationale: The response says organisations can disagree about current catastrophic-risk likelihood yet still agree on capability-triggered safeguards, calling this a more concrete basis for agreement across organisations with different views.
